title: Given a binary tree and a target sum, find all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values equals the target. Return the list of paths, and explain how backtracking lets you reuse one working list instead of copying at every node.
shortTitle: All Paths for a Sum (Collect Every Root-to-Leaf Path Matching a Target)

s1_definition.profdef: All Paths for a Sum extends the single-boolean path-sum problem into a collection problem. We perform a depth-first traversal, pushing each node's value onto a running path list as we descend and popping it as we return, which is the backtracking step. Whenever we reach a leaf whose accumulated sum equals the target, we take a defensive copy of the running path and add it to the results. Time is linear to visit the tree plus the cost of copying each qualifying path, and space is proportional to the tree height plus the stored results.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, instead of asking "does any approval chain cost exactly the budget," compliance now wants the full list of every approval chain whose fees add up to the budget. We walk down each chain writing the desk names on a notepad, and whenever a complete chain hits the budget we photocopy the notepad into our report. Then we erase the last desk and try the next branch, reusing the same notepad.
s1_definition.oneliner: Depth-first with a running path, copy the path at every matching leaf, and backtrack by removing the node on the way back up.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** All Paths for a Sum extends the single-boolean path-sum problem into a collection problem. We perform a depth-first traversal, pushing each node's value onto a running path list as we descend and popping it as we return, which is the backtracking step. Whenever we reach a leaf whose accumulated sum equals the target, we take a defensive copy of the running path and add it to the results. Time is linear to visit the tree plus the cost of copying each qualifying path, and space is proportional to the tree height plus the stored results.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, instead of asking "does any approval chain cost exactly the budget," compliance now wants the full list of every approval chain whose fees add up to the budget. We walk down each chain writing the desk names on a notepad, and whenever a complete chain hits the budget we photocopy the notepad into our report. Then we erase the last desk and try the next branch, reusing the same notepad.

**One line to remember:** Depth-first with a running path, copy the path at every matching leaf, and backtrack by removing the node on the way back up.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a single mutable list that represents the current path from the root to the node we are visiting. Before recursing into children we append the current node, for example `currentPath.add(node)`, and after both recursions return we remove it, for example `currentPath.remove(currentPath.size() - 1)`. This add-then-remove discipline is backtracking: the same list is reused for every path, which avoids allocating a fresh list at every node.

When we reach a leaf and the remaining target equals the leaf's value, we must store a snapshot, not the live list, for example `results.add(new ArrayList<>(currentPath))`. Forgetting the copy is the most common bug, because the live list keeps changing as backtracking continues, so all stored references would end up pointing at the same emptied list.

A senior-level nuance is that the total work is not simply linear when many paths qualify, because copying a path of length h costs O(h), and there can be up to O(n) leaves, giving O(n·h) in the worst case. That is inherent to returning the paths themselves rather than just a count. Another nuance is that we add the node to the path regardless of whether it is a leaf, and we only test the sum at a leaf, keeping the descent logic uniform.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compliance team audits Rajesh's transfer approval tree and needs the complete list of every root-to-leaf approval chain whose processing fees sum to the agreed budget. A single yes-or-no answer is no longer enough because auditors must document each acceptable chain by desk name. This is exactly how All Paths for a Sum works: each full desk chain is one path, and we collect every chain that hits the budget.

Problem 2 — Building a brand-new list for every desk we touch would waste memory on a deep hierarchy. This is why we keep one running desk list and backtrack, removing the last desk as we climb back, so memory stays proportional to the current depth rather than to the whole tree.

The code defines an `ApprovalNode` with a desk name and `BigDecimal` fee. An `AllPathsService` exposes `findAllChainsMatching(root, budget)` returning a list of desk-name lists. A `Demo` builds a tree where two separate chains both sum to the budget, proving the collector returns both.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Branch(100) root; Regional(250) left and Audit(200) right; SignA(50) under Regional's right; SignB(100) under Audit's left; budget 400.

Step 1: Enter Branch, path becomes [Branch], remaining after fee is 300. Not a matching leaf, so recurse left into Regional.

Step 2: Enter Regional, path becomes [Branch, Regional], remaining 50. Recurse into SignA.

Step 3: Enter SignA, path becomes [Branch, Regional, SignA], remaining 0. SignA is a leaf and remaining is zero, so we copy [Branch, Regional, SignA] into results. Backtrack removes SignA, then Regional, returning to Branch.

Step 4: Recurse right into Audit, path becomes [Branch, Audit], remaining 100. Recurse into SignB, path becomes [Branch, Audit, SignB], remaining 0, leaf matched, copy [Branch, Audit, SignB]. Backtrack all the way out.

Step 5: Final result holds both chains.

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:52:03 PM com.bank.approval.service.AllPathsService walk
FINE: At desk Branch remainingAfterFee=300
FINE: At desk Regional remainingAfterFee=50
FINE: At desk SignA remainingAfterFee=0
INFO: Matched chain: [Branch, Regional, SignA]
FINE: At desk Audit remainingAfterFee=100
FINE: At desk SignB remainingAfterFee=0
INFO: Matched chain: [Branch, Audit, SignB]
INFO: Found 2 matching approval chains
INFO: Matching chains for Rajesh SAV2001, budget 400: [[Branch, Regional, SignA], [Branch, Audit, SignB]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
All Paths for a Sum is the collection version of the path-sum problem: instead of a single boolean, I return every root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to the target. I solve it with a depth-first traversal that carries one running path list. As I descend I append the current node to that list and subtract its value from the target, and when I reach a leaf whose remaining target is zero I store a defensive copy of the list in my results. After exploring both children I remove the current node, which is the backtracking step that lets me reuse the same list for every path.

The detail I always stress is that I store a copy, not the live list. If I added the live reference, continued backtracking would keep mutating it, and every stored path would end up pointing at the same emptied list. I also note that returning the paths themselves is not strictly linear work, because copying a path of height h across up to n leaves gives O(n times h), and that cost is inherent to producing the paths rather than merely counting them.

At the National Bank of India I applied this to audit Rajesh's approval hierarchy, where compliance needed the full documented list of every desk chain whose processing fees summed exactly to the agreed budget. I modelled each desk as a node with a BigDecimal fee, drove the backtracking traversal from the top desk, and emitted each matching chain by desk name into the audit report. Describing the reuse-and-backtrack discipline together with the defensive copy is what tells an interviewer I can implement backtracking correctly under real auditing requirements rather than just recite the idea.
